newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Rebuilding begins on Angola's Benguela railway.
newsitem.headline: Rebuilding begins on Angola's Benguela railway.

text.p: After more than a decade of standing idle, Angola's war-battered Benguela railway line is expected to be carrying cargo between Angola's Lobito port and the nation's northern neighbour in the next three years.
Italy's Tor di Valle company has been charged with restoring 1,350 km (840 miles) of the railway line to the border, linking Lobito to the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire.
"We have agreed to make the minimum repairs to the line that will allow freight to start moving within three years," Claudio Insenga, Tor di Valle's representative in Angola, told Reuters.

Once Tor di Valle has restored the line to accommodate minimum traffic, it will modernise it by replacing the steel rails, reconstructing 22 passenger stations and three work stations, and rebuilding the telephone and signals system.

The Benguela railway was used extensively by colonial Portuguese until Angola's independence in 1975. A civil war that lasted 20 years between the MPLA-led government and rebel UNITA saw parts of the line destroyed in fighting.

The war ended in 1994 when both sides signed a peace pact which has been slow to take effect on the ground. A new unity government was installed in April this year and will remain in place until elections are held within four years.
RAILWAY KEY FOR MINERAL EXPORTS
The line previously carried copper and cobalt from Angola's landlocked eastern neighbour Zambia and from mines in the southern Zaire to Angolan ports.

Cobalt and copper exports from the former Zaire, mainly via Zambia, were disrupted by railway closures due to the country's seven-month-long civil war, which ended earlier this month with a rebel victory.
Zambia also stopped cross-border railway traffic with Kinshasa this month because of a dispute over debts.
"This railway is one of the keys to the reconstruction of the Angolan economy," Angola's Minister of Commerce, Vitorino Hossi, told Reuters.
"I can't tell you how important it is for us. With this railway Angola has a future."
Insenga said the port of Lobito was in good condition and could accommodate large freighters.
Though work is just beginning outside Lobito, Insenga says reconstruction of the line will be quick.

The 150 km (93 miles) from Lobito inland is in good condition, but a 400-km (250-mile) stretch between Cubal in Benguela province to Kuito in Bie province is in poor condition with four bridges destroyed.
Also in far eastern Moxico province, where rail coaches are home to Angolan refugees, the company will have to repair 20 bridges, Insenga said.
EUCALYPTUS EXPORT REVENUE SEEN COVERING COSTS
Land-mines placed on the line by rebels during the civil war will also have to be lifted.
Insenga said in exchange for reconstructing the railway line, the company will harvest for export a series of eucalyptus plantations, totalling some 37,000 hectares (92,500 acres).
The plantations, grown along the line, were developed by the Portuguese who used the wood to power steam engines.
Revenues from the forests are expected to generate more than $500 million, enough to cover the expenses of rehabilitating the railway line, Insenga said.
A study by South Africa's timber group, Sappi Ltd in 1996, however, found the eucalyptus project was not feasible.
Sappi researchers found that harvesting the timber would be too costly, given the total lack of infrastructure in the interior of Angola and the price fluctuations of eucalyptus on the open market.
But Tor di Valle said it expected to make a profit, although many of the forests around the central highlands capital of Humabo and nearby Kuito had been used as firewood by locals.
"The stands around Kuito and Huambo are in the worst condition by far," Insenga saod. "All of the others are in excellent condition."
Insenga said with the change in government in the former Zaire, the giant copper, gold and cobalt mines in the country's Shaba province will once again begin exporting through Angola.
